passages.text:
1.
Normal anatomy and histology Gross anatomy Anatomical feature Source-supported detail Overview The oesophagus is a muscular tube extending from the pharynx to the stomach.
Length Adult length: 25 cm (10 inches).
Incisor-to-LOS distance Distance from the incisors to the lower oesophageal sphincter: 40 cm.
Upper oesophageal sphincter The proximal oesophageal region at the cricopharyngeus is the upper oesophageal sphincter.
Lower oesophageal sphincter The portion adjacent to the anatomical gastro-oesophageal junction is the lower oesophageal sphincter (cardiac sphincter).
Constrictions Major constrictions shown: pharyngo-oesophageal at 16 cm, thoracic (aortobronchial) at 23 cm, and diaphragmatic near 38 cm; the abdominal oesophagus and cardiac stomach begin near 40 cm.
Histology Histological feature Source-supported detail Lining Lining: stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium.
Wall layers Wall layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria (muscularis externa), and adventitia/serosa in the intra-abdominal part.
2.
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) Physiology and pathophysiology
Between swallows, oesophageal muscles are relaxed except at the sphincters.
The lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) usually remains closed and relaxes when swallowing is initiated.
Transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations (TLESRs) are physiological but occur more frequently in GORD.
A small amount of reflux is normal.
Sphincter pressure rises in response to increased intra-abdominal and intragastric pressures.
Anti-reflux mechanisms
Main mechanisms: peristalsis, the diaphragm, the LOS, the intra-abdominal oesophageal segment, the mucosal valve, and unimpeded gastric emptying.
The intra-abdominal oesophageal segment acts as a flap valve.
A mucosal rosette formed by gastric mucosal folds and contraction of the crural diaphragm at the LOS acts like a pinchcock and prevents acid reflux.
A large hiatus hernia can impair this mechanism.
Refluxate is normally cleared rapidly by secondary peristalsis, gravity, and salivary bicarbonate.
Factors associated with reflux
Pregnancy and obesity.
Fat, chocolate, coffee, alcohol, and large meals.
Cigarette smoking.
Drugs: calcium-channel blockers and nitrates.
Systemic sclerosis.
After treatment of achalasia.
Hiatus hernia.
Oesophageal mucosal defence Defence level Source-supported details Surface defence Surface defence: mucus and the unstirred water layer trap bicarbonate; buffering is weak compared with the stomach and duodenum.
Epithelial defence
Epithelial defence: the apical cell membrane and junctional complexes limit H+ diffusion into cells.
In oesophagitis, junctional complexes are damaged.
Postepithelial defence
Postepithelial defence: bicarbonate normally buffers acid in cells and intracellular spaces.
Hydrogen ions impair growth and replication of damaged cells.
Sensory mechanism and pain
Sensory mechanism: acid activates primary sensory neurons through vanilloid receptor 1 (VR1).
This can initiate inflammation and release pro-inflammatory substances, producing pain.

passages.title: University Source · Passage 2
passages.text:
Defence level Source-supported details
Pain may also result from contraction of longitudinal oesophageal muscle.
2.
Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) — continued Clinical features Clinical domain Source-supported details Core symptoms and heartburn
The two principal clinical features are heartburn and regurgitation.
Heartburn is the major feature.
Heartburn is aggravated by bending, stooping, and lying down, which promote acid exposure.
Heartburn is relieved by oral antacids.
Patients may report pain after hot liquids or alcohol.
Correlation between heartburn and oesophagitis is poor.
Diagnostic difficulty and testing
Differentiating cardiac from oesophageal pain can be difficult.
A PPI trial is worthwhile; if symptoms persist, ambulatory pH and impedance monitoring should be performed.
Regurgitation and respiratory features
Regurgitation of food and acid occurs particularly when bending or lying flat.
Aspiration pneumonia is unusual without an accompanying stricture.
Cough and asthma can occur and may respond slowly to a PPI (1-4 months).
Alarm features and appearances
Alarm symptoms may indicate Barrett's oesophagus, oesophageal stricture, or oesophageal cancer.
Alarm symptoms: dysphagia, early satiety, GI bleeding, odynophagia, vomiting, unexplained weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, choking, and continual pain.
Endoscopic appearances shown include the gastro-oesophageal junction, an oesophageal ulcer, and streaking oesophagitis.
GORD pain versus cardiac ischaemia GORD pain Cardiac ischaemic pain
GORD pain is burning, worse on bending, stooping, or lying down, and seldom radiates to the arms.
GORD pain is worse with hot drinks or alcohol and is relieved by antacids.
Cardiac ischaemic pain is gripping or crushing, radiates to the neck or left arm, is worse with exercise, and is accompanied by dyspnoea.
Diagnosis and investigations Approach/test Role and source-supported findings Threshold or trace Clinical approach
A clinical diagnosis can be made.
Patients younger than 45 years without alarm signs, especially dysphagia, can initially be treated without investigations. — Endoscopy Endoscopy assesses oesophagitis and hiatus hernia. — Intraluminal monitoring
Intraluminal monitoring documents reflux.
Options include 24-hour luminal pH monitoring or impedance combined with manometry.
Monitoring is helpful when there is no response to PPI and should always confirm reflux before surgery.
Excessive reflux: pH <4 for >4% of the monitored time.
Illustrated trace: five reflux episodes with pH <4 occurred, but only three produced symptoms.
Treatment: lifestyle and procedures
Lose weight and raise the head end of the bed at night.
Avoid precipitating factors and use dietary measures.
Reduce alcohol and caffeine consumption and stop smoking.
Treatment categories: lifestyle modification, drugs, endoluminal gastroplication, and surgery.
Endoluminal gastroplication is an endoscopic procedure in which multiple plications or pleats are made below the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Surgery should not be performed for hiatus hernia alone.
The best surgical predictor is typical reflux symptoms with documented acid reflux.
Surgical technique: return the oesophageal junction to the abdominal cavity, mobilize the gastric fundus, close the diaphragmatic crura snugly, and create a short tension-free fundoplication.
Indications are not clear; considerations include intolerance to medication, desire for freedom from medication, treatment expense, and concern about long-term adverse effects.
Patients with oesophageal dysmotility unrelated to acid reflux, no response to PPIs, or underlying functional bowel disease should not have surgery.
Drug treatment Class Examples or dose Mechanism/use Cautions or outcome Overview Drug groups: alginate-containing antacids, dopamine-antagonist prokinetics, H2-receptor antagonists, proton-pump inhibitors, and the potassium-competitive acid blocker vonoprazan. — — Alginate-containing antacids Alginate-containing antacids: 10 mL three times daily; available over the counter.
Alginates form a gel or 'foam raft' with gastric contents to reduce reflux.
Magnesium-containing antacids tend to cause diarrhoea; aluminium-containing compounds cause constipation.

passages.text:
Class Examples or dose Mechanism/use Cautions or outcome Dopamine-antagonist prokinetics Metoclopramide and domepridone are dopamine-antagonist prokinetics that enhance peristalsis and accelerate gastric emptying. — — H2-receptor antagonists H2-receptor antagonists: cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine, and nizatidine.
H2-receptor antagonists suppress acid, are used if antacids fail, and are often available over the counter. — Proton-pump inhibitors PPIs listed: omeprazole, rabeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, and esomeprazole.
PPIs inhibit gastric hydrogen/potassium ATPase and reduce gastric acid secretion by 90%.
PPIs are the drug of choice for all mild cases; most patients respond well.
Heartburn persists in 20-30%; severe symptoms require twice-daily dosing and prolonged treatment.
Vonoprazan Vonoprazan is reported to be more potent than PPIs. — — Patterns among patients with reflux symptoms Phenotype/group Source-supported pattern Erosive oesophagitis Erosive oesophagitis: 20-30%; hiatus hernia 70%; pH-positive 75%; PPI response 90%.
Non-erosive reflux disease (NERD) Normal endoscopy occurs in 60-70% and represents non-erosive reflux disease (NERD), associated in the diagram with younger patients, women, and hiatus hernia in 30%.
Barrett's oesophagus Barrett's oesophagus: 6-12%; hiatus hernia 95%; pH-positive 75%. pH-positive NERD Among pH-positive NERD cases (60%), TLESRs are present and there is some PPI response. pH-negative functional group Among pH-negative cases (60%), the diagram labels the disorder 'functional'.
Hypersensitive oesophagus Of the pH-negative group, 40% have a hypersensitive oesophagus to minor pH changes with symptom index positive and some PPI response.
Functional heartburn The remaining 60% have functional heartburn driven by non-acid stimuli with a low PPI response.
Complications Aspect Source-supported detail Major complications Major complications: peptic stricture and Barrett's oesophagus.
Peptic stricture: occurrence Peptic strictures are uncommon in the PPI era and usually occur in patients older than 60 years.
Presentation Presentation: intermittent dysphagia for solids that worsens gradually over a long period.
Mild disease Mild cases may respond to PPI alone.
Severe disease Severe cases require endoscopic dilatation and long-term PPI therapy.
3.
Hiatus hernia Definition and pathogenesis
Hiatus hernia is herniation or protrusion of part of the stomach through the oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm.
Oesophageal hiatal hernia accounts for 98% of diaphragmatic hernias.
Congenital hiatal hernias occur in infants and children; many cases are acquired later in life.
Fewer than 10% of adults with a hiatal hernia are symptomatic, generally in association with other causes of LES incompetence.
Symptoms, including heartburn and regurgitation of gastric juice, resemble GORD.
The basic defect is failure of the diaphragmatic muscle fibres forming the oesophageal hiatus margin, due to congenital or acquired oesophageal shortening.
A congenitally short oesophagus accounts for a small proportion of cases.
Acquired causes include age-related muscle degeneration.
Acquired causes include raised intra-abdominal pressure, such as pregnancy or abdominal tumours.
Recurrent oesophageal regurgitation and spasm may cause inflammation, fibrosis, and oesophageal shortening.
Increased fatty tissue in obesity may reduce diaphragmatic muscular elasticity.
Anatomical patterns Type/frequency Anatomy GOJ/LOS position Clinical implication Sliding hernia
Sliding (oesophago-gastric) hernia is the commonest pattern (85%).
In a sliding hernia, the herniated stomach forms a supradiaphragmatic bell by sliding upward on both sides of the oesophagus.
In sliding hiatus hernia, the gastro-oesophageal junction and part of the stomach lie above the diaphragm.
Sliding hernia is present in 30% of people older than 50 years.
Sliding hernia produces no symptoms by itself; symptoms are due to reflux.

passages.text:
Type/frequency Anatomy GOJ/LOS position Clinical implication Rolling hernia
Rolling (para-oesophageal) hernia occurs in 10%; the gastric cardia rolls upward beside the oesophagus into an intrathoracic sac.
In rolling hernia, part of the fundus prolapses through the hiatus alongside the oesophagus.
The LOS remains below the diaphragm and remains competent in rolling hernia.
Occasionally, severe pain occurs because of volvulus or strangulation.
Mixed hernia Mixed (transitional) hernia accounts for the remaining 5% and combines sliding and rolling components. — — 4.
Barrett's oesophagus Definition and diagnosis Aspect Source-supported detail Definition Normal squamous oesophageal epithelium is replaced by metaplastic columnar mucosa, forming a segment of columnar-lined oesophagus (CLO).
Associated anatomy A hiatus hernia is almost always present.
Endoscopy Endoscopy shows proximal displacement of the squamocolumnar mucosal junction.
Biopsy Biopsy demonstrates columnar lining above the proximal gastric folds.
Diagnostic wording According to the British Society of Gastroenterology wording on the slide, intestinal metaplasia is no longer required for diagnosis.
Illustrated appearances The endoscopic images contrast normal lower oesophagus with Barrett's mucosa and show proximal abnormal mucosal extension and a Barrett's lesion.
Morphology and risk Morphology or risk factor Source-supported detail Circumferential sheet Barrett's mucosa may appear as a continuous circumferential sheet.
Finger-like projections It may form finger-like projections extending upward from the squamocolumnar junction.
Mucosal islands It may form islands of columnar mucosa within residual squamous mucosa.
Central obesity Central obesity increases the risk of Barrett's oesophagus 4.3-fold.
Typical patient group It is commonest in middle-aged obese men.
Adenocarcinoma risk Oesophageal adenocarcinoma develops in 0.12-0.5%.
5.
Eosinophilic oesophagitis Domain Source-supported detail Trend Its incidence is increasing markedly.
Adult presentation Adults present with food impaction and dysphagia.
Child presentation Children present with feeding intolerance or GORD-like symptoms.
Histology The cardinal histological feature is epithelial infiltration by numerous eosinophils, especially superficially and at sites far from the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Distinction from other disease Eosinophil abundance helps distinguish the condition from GORD, Crohn disease, and other causes of oesophagitis.
Clinical clues Typical clinical clues include failure of high-dose PPI treatment and absence of acid reflux.
Atopic associations Most affected patients are atopic; associations include atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, and modest peripheral eosinophilia.
Treatment Treatment includes dietary restriction of food allergens such as cow's milk and soy products, plus topical or systemic corticosteroids.
6.
Achalasia of the cardia History
In 1913, Ernest Heller performed the first surgical intervention; the procedure still carries his name.
Arthur Hurst used the term achalasia in a 1927 article on the treatment of 'cardiospasm'.
Achalasia is Greek for 'lack of relaxation'.
Ellis and colleagues described the first transthoracic approach in 1958.
Sir Alfred Cuschieri performed the first laparoscopic Heller myotomy in 1991.

passages.title: University Source · Passage 5
passages.text:
Definition and histopathology Feature Source-supported detail Core definition Achalasia consists of aperistalsis of the oesophageal body and a hypertonic lower oesophageal sphincter.
Neuronal degeneration It results from degeneration of neurons in the oesophageal wall.
Relative frequency It is the second most common benign oesophageal disorder requiring surgical intervention.
Myenteric plexus Histology shows decreased neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus.
Nitric-oxide-producing cells Nitric-oxide-producing cells, which contribute to LES relaxation, are preferentially depleted.
Cholinergic neurons Cholinergic neurons that maintain LES tone are relatively spared.
Functional consequence Loss of inhibitory neurons raises resting LES tone and causes oesophageal aperistalsis.
Aetiology Category Associations or mechanism Important clue Primary/immune associations
Primary achalasia is considered idiopathic.
HLA DQw1 and anti-myenteric antibodies have been associated with achalasia, supporting a proposed autoimmune mechanism. — Reported viral associations
Associations with chronic herpes zoster or measles have been reported.
T-cell reactivity to HSV-1 has been reported, suggesting a possible HSV-1-related mechanism. — Secondary achalasia: Chagas disease
Secondary achalasia may result from Chagas disease, which occurs mainly in Central and South America.
Chagas disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, carried by Rhodnius prolixus; the accompanying images show the parasite and vector.
Infection causes loss of ganglion cells in Auerbach's plexus. — Malignancy mimic Malignancy must be excluded because it can mimic achalasia.
Features suggesting malignancy: symptoms for <6 months, onset after age 60, excessive weight loss, and difficulty passing the endoscope through the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Incidence and clinical manifestations Clinical aspect Source-supported detail Annual incidence Annual incidence: 1.6 per 100,000 people.
Study limitation The relative rarity of achalasia makes it difficult to study compared with more common diseases.
Demographics It affects men and women equally and usually occurs at 20-50 years of age.
Dysphagia Dysphagia is the commonest symptom: food in >90% and liquids in >80%.
Comparison with dysmotility Other oesophageal dysmotility disorders may cause dysphagia, but not as frequently as achalasia.
Other manifestations Other manifestations: mild weight loss (usually <10 kg), regurgitation, chest pain, globus sensation, and hiccups.
Diagnosis Investigation/domain Characteristic findings Protected numbers or qualification General diagnostic course
Symptom onset is slow and gradual; the average interval from symptom onset to diagnosis is >4 years.
Three core diagnostic tools: barium swallow, endoscopy, and manometry. — Barium swallow Barium swallow is an excellent diagnostic tool; the classic appearance is a dilated oesophagus tapering to a 'bird's beak'.
Reported diagnostic accuracy of barium swallow: 95% in one study.
Manometry
Manometry finding 3: oesophageal aperistalsis; a swallow may produce no contraction or simultaneous contractions.
Contractions are classically low-amplitude, but high-amplitude simultaneous contractions define 'vigorous' achalasia.
Manometry finding 1: elevated resting LES pressure, often >45 mmHg.
Manometry finding 2: incomplete LES relaxation; normal relaxation should fall to <8 mmHg, whereas relaxation after a swallow may be incomplete or absent in achalasia.
Endoscopy
All patients with suspected achalasia should undergo upper-GI endoscopy to exclude malignancy.
At endoscopy, the oesophagus is usually enlarged and may contain retained food.

blocks.text: Definition and histopathology Feature Source-supported detail Core definition Achalasia consists of aperistalsis of the oesophageal body and a hypertonic lower oesophageal sphincter.
Neuronal degeneration It results from degeneration of neurons in the oesophageal wall.
Relative frequency It is the second most common benign oesophageal disorder requiring surgical intervention.
Myenteric plexus Histology shows decreased neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus.
Nitric-oxide-producing cells Nitric-oxide-producing cells, which contribute to LES relaxation, are preferentially depleted.
Cholinergic neurons Cholinergic neurons that maintain LES tone are relatively spared.
Functional consequence Loss of inhibitory neurons raises resting LES tone and causes oesophageal aperistalsis.
Aetiology Category Associations or mechanism Important clue Primary/immune associations
Primary achalasia is considered idiopathic.
HLA DQw1 and anti-myenteric antibodies have been associated with achalasia, supporting a proposed autoimmune mechanism. — Reported viral associations
Associations with chronic herpes zoster or measles have been reported.
T-cell reactivity to HSV-1 has been reported, suggesting a possible HSV-1-related mechanism. — Secondary achalasia: Chagas disease
Secondary achalasia may result from Chagas disease, which occurs mainly in Central and South America.
Chagas disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, carried by Rhodnius prolixus; the accompanying images show the parasite and vector.
Infection causes loss of ganglion cells in Auerbach's plexus. — Malignancy mimic Malignancy must be excluded because it can mimic achalasia.
Features suggesting malignancy: symptoms for <6 months, onset after age 60, excessive weight loss, and difficulty passing the endoscope through the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Incidence and clinical manifestations Clinical aspect Source-supported detail Annual incidence Annual incidence: 1.6 per 100,000 people.
Study limitation The relative rarity of achalasia makes it difficult to study compared with more common diseases.
Demographics It affects men and women equally and usually occurs at 20-50 years of age.
Dysphagia Dysphagia is the commonest symptom: food in >90% and liquids in >80%.
Comparison with dysmotility Other oesophageal dysmotility disorders may cause dysphagia, but not as frequently as achalasia.
Other manifestations Other manifestations: mild weight loss (usually <10 kg), regurgitation, chest pain, globus sensation, and hiccups.
Diagnosis Investigation/domain Characteristic findings Protected numbers or qualification General diagnostic course
Symptom onset is slow and gradual; the average interval from symptom onset to diagnosis is >4 years.

Three core diagnostic tools: barium swallow, endoscopy, and manometry. — Barium swallow Barium swallow is an excellent diagnostic tool; the classic appearance is a dilated oesophagus tapering to a 'bird's beak'.
Reported diagnostic accuracy of barium swallow: 95% in one study.
Manometry
Manometry finding 3: oesophageal aperistalsis; a swallow may produce no contraction or simultaneous contractions.
Contractions are classically low-amplitude, but high-amplitude simultaneous contractions define 'vigorous' achalasia.
Manometry finding 1: elevated resting LES pressure, often >45 mmHg.
Manometry finding 2: incomplete LES relaxation; normal relaxation should fall to <8 mmHg, whereas relaxation after a swallow may be incomplete or absent in achalasia.
Endoscopy
All patients with suspected achalasia should undergo upper-GI endoscopy to exclude malignancy.
At endoscopy, the oesophagus is usually enlarged and may contain retained food.
The LES does not open spontaneously but can be traversed with gentle pressure. — Additional imaging CT or endoscopic ultrasound may help if another cause, such as malignancy, is suspected. —

passages.title: University Source · Passage 6
passages.text:
6.
Achalasia of the cardia — treatment Medical therapy Aspect Source-supported detail Drug and timing Calcium-channel blockers or nitrates are taken 10-30 minutes before meals.
Role and limitation They have moderate success but require perpetual use and are not recommended as first-line therapy.
Botulinum toxin (BOTOX) Aspect Source-supported detail Mechanism Botulinum neurotoxin type A inhibits acetylcholine release.
Intended balance Blocking presynaptic acetylcholine release in Auerbach's plexus is intended to restore neurotransmitter balance.
Delivery BOTOX is injected endoscopically into the LES.
Standard technique Standard technique: 1 mL (20-25 units BT/mL) into each of four quadrants about 1 cm above the Z-line.
Complications Complications: mediastinitis, oesophageal mucosal ulceration, and pneumothorax.
Outcome over time Symptomatic relief may reach 90% after a few months but falls to 50% or less at 1 year and continues to decline.
Recommended role Consensus in the lecture: reserve BOTOX for patients unfit for other interventions.
Pneumatic dilatation Aspect Source-supported detail Role Pneumatic dilatation is considered the most effective non-surgical treatment.
Technique The balloon is positioned across the LES using endoscopy and fluoroscopy.
Pressure Inflation pressure: 7-15 psi.
Observation Patients are usually observed for 6 hours and then discharged.
Predictors of success Best predictors of success: post-dilatation pressure (or the pre/post pressure difference) and older age.
Perforation risk The main concern is oesophageal perforation; reported rates range from 1.6% to about 10%, with one study reporting 21%.
Heller myotomy and fundoplication Domain Source-supported details Historical and current technique
Heller's original 1913 operation used an abdominal approach with anterior and posterior oesophagomyotomy.
Current surgery usually performs only an anterior myotomy through an abdominal or thoracic approach; laparoscopic and thoracoscopic approaches are described.
The thoracic approach has drawbacks.
Laparoscopic myotomy is considered the standard operation, with complication rates similar to open surgery but shorter hospital stay and recovery.
Operative questions and antireflux rationale
Key operative questions: whether to add fundoplication, which fundoplication, management of sigmoid oesophagus, myotomy length, and possible robotic benefit.
Without an antireflux procedure, 30% reported significant heartburn and objective pH/endoscopy evidence of reflux occurred in 60%.
The cited analysis recommends a concurrent antireflux procedure with laparoscopic Heller myotomy.
Dor versus Toupet
Dor fundoplication is an anterior 180-degree wrap.
Toupet fundoplication is a posterior 270-degree wrap.
The lecture reports no significant difference between Dor and Toupet for dysphagia, GORD, or PPI use.
At the time of the cited slide, no randomized controlled trial had compared Dor and Toupet.
Sigmoid oesophagus
Achalasic sigmoid oesophagus is markedly dilated, tortuous, and angulated.
It was previously thought to require oesophagectomy or at least preclude fundoplication.
Myotomy length and later reports
Commonly quoted myotomy length: 5 cm on the oesophagus plus 1 cm onto the cardia.
A 2007 retrospective review reported superior long-term efficacy with extended Heller myotomy plus Toupet fundoplication.
A 2006 report described robot-assisted laparoscopic Heller myotomy as safe and effective.
Peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM)
POEM is a submucosal endoscopic oesophageal myotomy first presented in the lecture as a novel experimental approach (Endoscopy, 2007).
POEM is considered a form of NOTES.
The lecture identifies Dr Haruhiro Inoue as the leading expert and states that he had performed >100 procedures.

passages.title: University Source · Passage 7
passages.text:
Enter the submucosal space about 15 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction using an endoscope with a transparent cap.
Saline with indigo dye is used to create a tunnel extending to about 2 cm beyond the gastro-oesophageal junction.
Myotomy begins about 10 cm proximal to the gastro-oesophageal junction and continues to 2 cm beyond it.
Only inner circular fibres are divided; outer longitudinal fibres remain intact.
The endoscope is removed from the tunnel and the entry site is closed with endoscopic clips.
Treatment algorithm and summary Modality/domain Source-supported summary Medical therapy Medical nitrates/CCBs are used primarily in older patients who cannot undergo surgery.
BOTOX BOTOX injection is endoscopic, time-limited, and requires repeat injections.
Pneumatic dilatation
The algorithm reports good long-term outcome in 50% after pneumatic dilatation, lists advanced achalasia as a contraindication, and gives a 7% perforation rate.
Pneumatic dilatation is effective but carries a perforation risk.
Heller myotomy
Heller myotomy is presented as the primary treatment for most operable symptomatic patients; it is an extramucosal cardiomyotomy with good results in >85%.
The algorithm recommends laparoscopic Heller myotomy plus partial fundoplication to reduce reflux after myotomy.
Laparoscopic Heller myotomy has excellent results and should be accompanied by Dor or Toupet fundoplication, not Nissen.
The summary recommends myotomy of at least 5 cm on the oesophagus and 2 cm on the stomach, possibly longer.
Advanced disease Oesophagectomy may be required in very advanced cases with megaoesophagus.
Cancer surveillance The lecture states a 3-5% risk of squamous-cell carcinoma in achalasia; risk does not decrease after successful myotomy, so periodic oesophagoscopy is advised.
Core mechanism Overall mechanism: myenteric plexus disease causes high resting LES pressure and oesophageal aperistalsis.
Overall treatment positioning Medical therapy is ineffective; BOTOX is reserved for patients unable to undergo other interventions.
Future and POEM
The robot may have a future role.
POEM shows promise, but the lecture notes insufficient long-term results and comparative studies for definitive conclusions.
